templates.one_move_blunder: {played_san} hangs your {hung_piece} on {hung_square}, and after {opp_reply_san} you simply lose it for nothing; better was {best_san}, since {best_purpose}. Before you commit a move, check what your opponent can capture and count the trade first.
templates.walked_into_tactic: {front}; instead {best_san} was stronger because {best_purpose}, whereas {played_san} hands material away. Before any quiet move, check that it doesn't walk into a tactic that drops a piece.
templates.missed_free_material: {played_san} isn't a blunder, but {best_san} {win}, so you left material on the board. When an enemy piece sits undefended, grab it before making a quiet developing move.
templates.missed_mate: Instead of {played_san}, {best_san} was far stronger, throwing a forcing move at the exposed king and keeping the attack rolling. Always look hard at your checks and forcing moves before settling for a quieter line.
templates.allowed_mate: {played_san} lets your opponent force mate, so play {best_san} instead to shore up your king's safety. Before every move, ask what checks and captures your opponent gets.
templates.opening_knowledge: Your {played_san} brings the queen out too early, so Black can attack it with tempo and force a retreat while gaining development. Play {best_san} instead—it develops with purpose, fights for the center, and keeps your queen safe; develop your pieces before chasing with the queen.

good_move_templates.develop: {move} brings your {piece} out to {to_square} and gets it into the game — in the opening, develop your knights and bishops off the back row early so you can castle and fight for the center.
good_move_templates.pawn: {move} puts your {piece} on {to_square} to fight for space and open good squares for your other pieces; in the opening, make moves that give your pieces room to come out and join the game.
good_move_templates.capture: {move} snaps up the {piece} on {to_square} for free, winning material — when an enemy piece sits with nothing guarding it and it is safe to take, take it.
good_move_templates.other: {move} repositions your {piece} to {to_square}, a safer and more useful square — good habit: place each piece where it stays safe while doing the most work.
good_move_templates.castle: {move}: {piece} castles to safety on {to_square}, tucking your king into the corner and bringing a rook toward the center — castle early to get your king safe before the position opens up.
good_move_templates.centralize: {move} centralizes your {piece} on {to_square}, an active central square where it controls more of the board — put your pieces on central squares where they influence the most.
good_move_templates.queen_safety: {move} brings your {piece} back to {to_square}, off the open line and out of danger onto a calm square connected to your other pieces — when a piece feels exposed, move it to safety before pushing your own plans.
good_move_templates.space: {move} pushes your {piece} to {to_square}, grabbing space on that part of the board and giving your pieces room — when a pawn push gains space safely, it is usually worth playing.
good_move_templates.luft: {move} advances your {piece} to {to_square}, giving your king a little breathing room and denying your opponent a useful square — when nothing is urgent, quietly improving your king's safety is a good use of a move.
good_move_templates.rook_activity: {move} brings your {piece} to {to_square} where it stays active on a real target instead of sitting idle — put your rooks where they stay mobile and threaten something.
good_move_templates.rook_open_file: {move} brings your {piece} to {to_square}, seizing an open file where it controls the most squares — place your rooks on open files (columns with no pawns), where they reach the farthest.
